What is a Servlet and a Servlet container?

A Servlet is a Java class that handles requests and generates responses (jakarta.servlet.Servlet). The container (Tomcat, Jetty, Undertow) manages the servlet lifecycle, maps URLs, manages threads and sessions, and enforces security. Spring MVC's DispatcherServlet is itself a servlet.
Explain the servlet lifecycle.
Load the class → create one instance → init() once → service() for each request, on a separate thread, dispatching to doGet, doPost and so on → destroy() once at undeploy or shutdown.
GenericServlet vs HttpServlet?

GenericServlet is protocol-independent and abstract, and you implement service(). HttpServlet extends it for HTTP and dispatches to doGet, doPost, doPut, doDelete based on the HTTP method. You almost always extend HttpServlet.
GET vs POST?

GET | POST
Data goes in the URL query string | Data goes in the body
Idempotent, cacheable, can be bookmarked | Not idempotent, not cached
Limited by URL length | No practical limit; can carry binary/multipart
For reading | For creating or submitting
ServletConfig vs ServletContext?

ServletConfig belongs to a single servlet: its init params, available in init(). ServletContext is one per web application and shared by all servlets: app-wide params, attributes, resources, and logging. The application scope in JSP is the ServletContext.
How is session management done? (HTTP is stateless)

- Cookies (the JSESSIONID cookie)
- URL rewriting (;jsessionid=…, using response.encodeURL)
- Hidden form fields
- HttpSession API: req.getSession(), setAttribute, invalidate(), and a timeout (<session-timeout>)
Modern REST APIs are stateless and use JWT tokens instead.
RequestDispatcher forward vs include vs sendRedirect?

- forward: hands the request to another resource on the server. The browser URL doesn't change, it's one request, and the response must not be committed yet.
- include: inserts the other resource's output into the current response.
- sendRedirect: sends a 302 to the browser, which makes a new request. It can point to an external URL, and request attributes are lost.
What are Filters and Listeners?

Filter: intercepts requests and responses before and after the servlet. Used for authentication, logging, compression, CORS and encoding. It's the Chain of Responsibility pattern, and Spring Security is built as a filter chain.
Listener: reacts to lifecycle events: ServletContextListener (app start and stop), HttpSessionListener (session created or destroyed), ServletRequestListener, and attribute listeners.
Are servlets thread-safe?

No. There's one instance and many threads, so instance variables are shared. Keep servlets stateless and use local variables. If shared state is unavoidable, use synchronized blocks or concurrent classes. (SingleThreadModel was deprecated and removed in Servlet 6.0.)
What is load-on-startup?

Tells the container to create and init() the servlet at deployment, so the first request isn't slow. A value ≥ 0 enables it, and lower numbers load first. A negative value or no value means lazy loading.
What is the difference between javax.servlet and jakarta.servlet?
Java EE moved to the Eclipse Foundation and was renamed Jakarta EE. Starting with Jakarta EE 9, the packages changed from javax.* to jakarta.*. Spring Boot 3 and Tomcat 10+ require jakarta.*.
Why is HttpServlet abstract when it has no abstract methods?

Every doXxx has a working default (405, or the OPTIONS and TRACE logic), so the compiler wouldn't require anything. It's marked abstract so you can't deploy it directly, which would be pointless since it serves nothing. You're forced to subclass and override at least one method.
What happens if you override service() and doGet() both?

service() runs and doGet doesn't, unless your override calls super.service(req, res). The dispatch logic lives in the method you replaced. Overriding service is reasonable only when you want one method to handle every HTTP verb, such as an error servlet.
Can a servlet have a constructor? Can it have constructor arguments?

Yes, but the container calls the public no-argument one. If you add only a constructor with arguments, there's no no-arg constructor, so instantiation fails. Even in the no-arg constructor getServletConfig() returns null, so initialisation belongs in init(). With programmatic registration (ctx.addServlet("x", new MyServlet(dep))) you create the instance yourself, and that's how Spring passes dependencies into DispatcherServlet.
Is init() called once per servlet class?

Once per servlet declaration. Two <servlet> entries with the same class create two objects with two init calls. Also, if init throws ServletException the instance is discarded, and the container can create a new one and try again on the next request, which Tomcat 11 did in a test.
getParameter() vs getAttribute()?

getParameter reads data the client sent (query string or form body). It returns a String and there's no setParameter. getAttribute reads objects that server code stored with setAttribute, typically a servlet passing data to a JSP. It returns Object and exists only for the request's lifetime.
Why does request.getParameter return null for my JSON POST?

getParameter parses the query string and application/x-www-form-urlencoded (and multipart with config). A JSON body has neither, so you must read it: mapper.readValue(req.getReader(), Dto.class). On Tomcat 11, a POST to ?a=q with JSON body {"a":2} gave getParameter("a") = q, and the body was untouched.
Output: what does the client see? res.getWriter().print("LOST "); dispatcher.forward(req, res); res.getWriter().print(" AFTER");

Only the target's output. forward clears uncommitted buffered output, so "LOST " is gone. The container closes the response when the forward returns, so " AFTER" is discarded too, although the line still runs. On Tomcat 11 a filter that printed before and after the servlet also lost its output, for the same reason.
What if you flush and then call forward or sendRedirect?

Both throw IllegalStateException, because headers have gone out. Tomcat 11's messages are "Cannot forward after response has been committed" and "Cannot call sendRedirect() after the response has been committed". The client keeps a 200 with the partial body. That's a common bug in large pages: the error happens after the buffer has overflowed and no error page can appear. A larger buffer postpones the commit.
sendError() vs setStatus()?

setStatus only sets the code, and you still write the body. sendError clears the buffer, commits the response, and hands over to the error page mechanism. It throws IllegalStateException if the response is committed. Don't write after it.
Why does a redirect after POST use 303 and not 302?

The HTTP spec originally said a 302 should keep the method, but browsers changed POST to GET, and 303 was added to state that intent exactly. In practice sendRedirect's 302 works for PRG, but 303 is the precise code: res.setStatus(303); res.setHeader("Location", url);, or the Servlet 6.1 overload sendRedirect(url, 303). Use 307 or 308 when the method and body must be kept.
Is HttpSession created automatically?

A servlet creates a session only if code calls getSession() or getSession(true). A JSP creates one by default because the session implicit object is on unless <%@ page session="false" %> is set. Unexpected Set-Cookie: JSESSIONID in a REST API usually comes from a JSP, a framework or a stray getSession(), and it wastes memory.
What's the difference between session timeout and cookie max-age?

Session timeout is an idle limit on the server, reset by each request. The default is 30 minutes in Tomcat; <session-timeout> takes minutes and setMaxInactiveInterval takes seconds (30 in web.xml reported 1800 at runtime). The JSESSIONID cookie normally has no max-age, so the browser deletes it when closed, leaving the server copy to expire. In web.xml a timeout of zero or less means the session never times out, and that's a memory leak.
What is session fixation and how do you prevent it?

The attacker gets a valid session ID and tricks the victim into using it, for instance through a ;jsessionid= link. After the victim logs in, that same ID is authenticated and the attacker can use it. Change the ID at login with req.changeSessionId(), which keeps the attributes. Spring Security does this by default. Also disable URL tracking with <tracking-mode>COOKIE</tracking-mode>.
How are cookies and sessions different?

A cookie is a small value stored by the browser (about 4 KB per cookie), visible to the client and sent with each request. A session is data held on the server and found through an ID, usually inside a cookie. Sensitive data belongs in the session, or in a signed or encrypted token if stateless.
Can a filter run without a servlet? What about for a static file?

Yes. The chain always ends at some resource, and for static files that's the container's default servlet, so /* filters run for CSS and images. A filter can also generate the entire response itself and never call the chain.
Why doesn't my filter run on a forward?

A filter's default dispatcher type is REQUEST only. Add it: @WebFilter(urlPatterns = "/*", dispatcherTypes = {DispatcherType.REQUEST, DispatcherType.FORWARD}), or <dispatcher>FORWARD</dispatcher> in the mapping. Be careful to avoid double work: a filter that runs on both will run twice for one user request, and OncePerRequestFilter guards against this.
Why can't you set a response header after chain.doFilter()?

Often the servlet has written enough to flush, or the container has committed the response, so headers have gone. Calls to setHeader on a committed response are silently ignored. Solutions: set the header before the chain, or pass a response wrapper with a buffer so nothing commits until you decide.
How would you compress or modify a response in a filter?

Pass a HttpServletResponseWrapper down the chain. Override getWriter and getOutputStream so that the servlet writes into your stream, a GZIPOutputStream or an in-memory buffer. After the chain returns, finish the stream or transform the buffer and write it to the real response. It's the Decorator pattern. In practice, enable compression in the connector (server.compression.enabled=true) or at the proxy.
How do you log request bodies in a filter without breaking the app?

The body stream can only be read once. Wrap the request in a class that buffers the bytes and returns a fresh ServletInputStream on each getInputStream call, or use Spring's ContentCachingRequestWrapper, which caches as the application reads, so you log after chain.doFilter. Cap the size, skip multipart, and mask passwords.
How can 10,000 clients stay connected to a Tomcat with 200 threads?

The NIO connector separates connections from threads. Idle keep-alive sockets are watched by one Poller using a Selector. A worker is used only while a request is being processed. maxConnections (8192 by default) limits open sockets and maxThreads (200) limits active processing. If all 200 workers are busy, ready sockets wait for a free worker. Blocking calls in your code are what really exhaust the pool.
Tomcat is up but requests hang. How do you diagnose it?

- Take a thread dump (jstack, jcmd <pid> Thread.print) and look at the http-nio-*-exec-* threads.
- If all are in HikariPool.getConnection, the DB pool is exhausted, probably from a leak or slow queries.
- If they're in socket read, a downstream call has no timeout.
- If they're BLOCKED on a monitor, there's a contention point such as a synchronized method.
- Check the busy-thread count via JMX or Actuator (tomcat.threads.busy).
- Fix the cause: timeouts, query tuning, a bulkhead around slow dependencies. Raising maxThreads alone only delays failure.
Does async processing make the request faster?

No, the client waits just as long, and each request has some added overhead. It improves throughput under waiting by releasing the container thread during slow I/O. It helps only if the wait doesn't merely move to another thread: 200 tasks on an executor that blocks 200 threads has saved nothing unless those threads use non-blocking I/O or are virtual threads. For CPU-bound work it gives no benefit.
What's the difference between AsyncContext.complete() and dispatch()?

complete() means the response is finished, so the container commits and ends the request. dispatch() re-enters the container on a container thread with DispatcherType.ASYNC so a servlet or JSP can produce the output. Filters run again if they include ASYNC. Spring MVC uses dispatch() for Callable: the worker gets the result, then a second pass through DispatcherServlet renders it. Calling neither makes the request hang until the timeout.
How do virtual threads change servlet thread safety and pool sizing?

Thread safety is unchanged: the same servlet instance is still shared and fields are still dangerous. Sizing changes: with one cheap virtual thread per request (Java 21+), maxThreads stops being the limit, so the limit moves to other resources such as the DB pool. Concurrency may need explicit limits (a Semaphore) to protect downstream systems. Heavy use of per-thread caches stops making sense. Java 21 pins a virtual thread to its carrier inside synchronized blocks during blocking; Java 24 removed that limitation for most cases.
How do you share data between two servlets?

Pick the narrowest scope. Request attributes when forwarding; session attributes for one user's requests; ServletContext attributes for the whole app on one node; a database or cache for everything across nodes. Query params or cookies are for carrying small data over a redirect.
Can you call one servlet's doGet from another directly?

It's a protected method, and the servlet instance is owned by the container, so direct calls are wrong: you'd bypass filters and any setup. Use a RequestDispatcher, or better, move the shared logic to a plain service class called by both servlets.

What's a RequestDispatcher, and how do you get a named one?

An object wrapping a target resource that can be forwarded to or included. req.getRequestDispatcher(path) accepts a relative path. ctx.getRequestDispatcher(path) needs a leading /. ctx.getNamedDispatcher("servletName") locates by name. All return null if nothing matches. With a named dispatcher the forward attributes aren't set, because the path doesn't change.
Why is a servlet in a WAR unreachable under WEB-INF, and why is that useful?

The container refuses direct client requests for WEB-INF and META-INF content. But a server-side forward can reach them. So put JSPs in /WEB-INF/views/ and users must go through a controller that does authorisation and loads data, instead of opening the view directly.
Explain the startup of a Spring Boot embedded Tomcat app in servlet terms.

- Spring Boot creates the application context, then an embedded Tomcat object through TomcatServletWebServerFactory.
- It adds a Context and registers all ServletContextInitializer beans.
- DispatcherServletRegistrationBean maps DispatcherServlet to /, and each Filter bean is registered through FilterRegistrationBean or by default adaptation.
- Boot's embedded setup doesn't scan for @WebServlet unless you add @ServletComponentScan, and ServletContainerInitializer from the classpath isn't run by default.
So the servlet model is intact, only inverted: the app starts the container, and not the other way around.
A @WebServlet returns 404 after deployment. Checklist?

- Context path wrong? The URL needs /app/x, not /x, unless deployed as ROOT.
- Was the class deployed, and is it in WEB-INF/classes?
- metadata-complete="true" in web.xml turns scanning off.
- Is it a javax.servlet class on Tomcat 10+? The container won't recognise it, so the annotation is ignored.
- In Spring Boot, is @ServletComponentScan missing?
- Did startup fail? Check catalina.out.
Design: how would you implement a rate limiter or request ID in the servlet layer?

Use a filter, since it runs before all servlets, can reject early and can see the raw request. For request ID: read or generate an ID, put it in the MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context, a logging ThreadLocal), add it to the response header before chain.doFilter, and clear the MDC in finally. For rate limiting: key by authenticated user or a trusted client IP, count in Redis so that all nodes share the limit, and return 429 with Retry-After. Don't call the chain when the limit is hit. Order it after authentication if you key by user, and consider async requests where the MDC doesn't propagate.
What's the difference between a web server, a servlet container, and an application server?

A web server (nginx, Apache httpd) serves static content and proxies. A servlet container (Tomcat, Jetty) runs the servlet, JSP, EL and WebSocket specs. An application server (WildFly, Payara) implements Jakarta EE fully, with CDI, JPA, JMS and JTA. Tomcat also includes an HTTP server, so nginx in front is optional but common for TLS, caching and load balancing.
no-cache vs no-store?

no-store means the response must not be stored anywhere, which is right for sensitive data. no-cache means it may be stored but must be revalidated with the server (via ETag or Last-Modified) before each reuse, so a 304 can save bandwidth. For fingerprinted static files use a long max-age with immutable.
How do ETags and conditional requests work?

The server sends an ETag identifying the version of a resource. The client later sends If-None-Match: "etag"; if the version is unchanged the server returns 304 with no body. For updates, If-Match enables optimistic concurrency: a PUT with a stale ETag gets 412 Precondition Failed.
How does a WebSocket connection start, and how is it different from SSE?

It starts as an HTTP GET with Upgrade: websocket and Sec-WebSocket-Key; the server responds 101 Switching Protocols and the connection becomes a full-duplex message channel. SSE is one-way (server to client) over plain HTTP, with automatic reconnect, and is simpler through proxies. Use WebSockets for chat or collaborative editing, SSE for notifications and progress updates.
Why does getParameter() return null for a PUT with a form body?

The Servlet spec only requires the container to parse application/x-www-form-urlencoded bodies into parameters for POST. For PUT or PATCH, read the body yourself, use JSON, or in Spring add FormContentFilter (enabled by default in Spring Boot), which parses form bodies for PUT, PATCH and DELETE.
Why do non-English characters appear garbled?

The encoding wasn't set at the right time. setCharacterEncoding("UTF-8") must run before any parameter is read, and the response charset must be set before getWriter() is called. Also check the DB connection and column charset (utf8mb4) and the HTML meta charset. Spring Boot sets UTF-8 by default through its encoding filter.
How do you get the real client IP behind a load balancer?

Proxies put the original address in X-Forwarded-For (a comma-separated chain) or the standard Forwarded header. Configure Tomcat's RemoteIpValve or server.forward-headers-strategy=native/framework in Spring Boot with the trusted proxy ranges, so getRemoteAddr(), scheme and HTTPS detection are correct. Never trust the header blindly, because clients can spoof it.
How do you handle a CORS preflight in a servlet filter?

For non-simple requests (JSON body, custom headers like Authorization) the browser first sends OPTIONS with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method. The filter checks the origin against an allowlist, returns Access-Control-Allow-Origin, -Methods, -Headers and optionally -Max-Age with 200/204, and doesn't pass the preflight to the servlet. With cookies you need Allow-Credentials: true and a specific origin, never *. In Spring Security configure http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()) with a CorsConfigurationSource bean so preflights aren't blocked by authentication.
Does HTTP/2 change how you write servlets?

Mostly no: the servlet API is the same, and the container handles multiplexing many streams over one connection, header compression and binary framing. Benefits are fewer connections and no head-of-line blocking at the HTTP level, which reduces the need for tricks like domain sharding and sprite bundling. Server push existed in Servlet 4 but browsers dropped it and it was deprecated, so don't rely on it. HTTP/2 is often terminated at the proxy or load balancer.
Request vs session vs application attributes: lifetime and thread safety?

| Request | Session | Application (ServletContext)
Set with | request.setAttribute | session.setAttribute | context.setAttribute
Lives for | One request, including forwards and includes | One user, until timeout or invalidate() | The whole web app, until undeploy
Visible to | That request only | All requests carrying that session id | Every request of every user
Thread safety | Safe, one thread (unless you go async) | Not safe: one user can send parallel requests | Not safe: use thread-safe objects
Survives redirect? | No | Yes | Yes
Rule of thumb: pick the shortest scope that works. Session data should be small and Serializable if the app is clustered; application data should be read-only or a concurrent structure.
getWriter() vs getOutputStream()?
Thread-per-request vs async servlet vs virtual threads?

| Classic blocking | Async servlet | Virtual threads
While waiting on I/O | A platform thread is held | The container thread is released | The virtual thread unmounts from its carrier
Code style | Simple, blocking | startAsync(), callbacks, complete() | Simple, blocking
Concurrency limit | Thread pool size (Tomcat default max 200) | Your own executor and timeouts | Mostly downstream limits like the DB pool
Faster single request? | No | No | No
Watch out for | Pool exhaustion on slow calls | Forgetting complete() or a timeout | ThreadLocal caches, pinning on JDKs before 24
Rule of thumb: on Java 21+ virtual threads give async-level scalability with blocking code. Async servlets still make sense for long-polling and server push. None of them makes shared servlet fields thread-safe.
WAR on an external Tomcat vs an executable JAR with embedded Tomcat?

| WAR on external server | Executable JAR (embedded)
Who owns the container | Ops, shared by many apps | The app, one container per app
Container version | Same for every app on the server | Chosen per app in the build
Startup | Container scans and deploys the WAR | main() starts the container
Config | server.xml, context.xml, JNDI | application.properties
Fits | Legacy estates, app-server standards | Docker, Kubernetes, microservices
Rule of thumb: new Spring Boot services ship as a JAR in a container image. To build a WAR from Boot, extend SpringBootServletInitializer and mark the embedded Tomcat dependency as provided.
